extracted.intended_audience: College mathematics instructors and teacher-educators implementing active learning and equitable participation strategies
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for structuring partner, group, and whole-class interactions to promote equitable participation, productive mathematical talk, and formative peer feedback in college math classrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default to partner work for short interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want students to engage with peers, and you only have a small amount of time, default to partner work due to its flexibility and ease of implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partner work for quick checks when presenting a proof (e.g., justify why a step works, clarify a definition, or come up with an example). Benefits: builds community, surfaces who is following along, lowers threat for asking questions, and provides access for anxious students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit framing for partner discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: Using explicit framing can help prevent a single student from dominating a partner discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear turn-taking instructions and timing (example script: 'The first partner will talk for a minute to share their idea, and then when the timer goes off, the peer will have a minute to respond. Please don’t interrupt your peer during their talk time.'). More important than any particular structure is that explicit instructions help ensure all students get to talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use partner work for structured peer feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Partner work is effective for swapping partial solutions and exchanging feedback in a way that typically does not work as well in larger groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students exchange partial solutions and provide structured feedback. This is particularly effective for short cycles of formative feedback and peer critique; see Section 6.3.2 (referenced) for more on peer feedback practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use partner discussion as a pre-check before whole-class
rubrics_metrics.description: A short partner discussion before a whole-class discussion helps ensure every student has at least something to share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask students 'what they talked about' rather than 'what the answer is' to focus on process rather than product and to lower barriers for sharing in the public sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use group work for messy, open-ended problems (3–5 students, 15–30+ minutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Group work with unstructured problems is appropriate when you want small teams (ideally 3–5) to work on messy, open-ended tasks for an extended time (15–30 minutes or more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group tasks develop authentic problem-solving skills and show the 'messiness of mathematics.' Because group work requires more setup, prefer individual or partner work if a task is simple. Foster productive struggle for challenging tasks (see Section 4.4.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-and-release to address common group questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When many groups ask the same question, use a catch-and-release strategy to address it collectively rather than answering repeatedly at the group level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an attention-getter (e.g., speaking loudly, flicking lights) to bring class together, answer the question for everyone, then release them to continue. This saves time and helps groups stay productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of group composition to mitigate inequities
rubrics_metrics.description: Group composition matters: students with more axes of privilege are more likely to dominate small-group conversations, so attend to gender, race, language, disability, and other identities when forming groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid configurations that surround a single minoritized student with students from dominant groups. Strategies: pseudo-random assignment (randomize then reconfigure non-ideal arrangements), sometimes place minoritized students together (rather than always splitting them up), and solicit student input (survey questions such as 'What’s working well in your current group?', 'Would you like to change groups?'). Research shows women have more participation when in majority-women groups; be mindful of these patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use semi-stable groups and reconfigure infrequently
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain groups for a few weeks to build positive interdependence, but mix them up occasionally to avoid groups getting stuck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semi-stable groups combine benefits of stable social relations with opportunities to break up dysfunctional groups. Experiment locally and use brief questionnaires or Google Forms to guide reconfiguration decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign structured group roles and rotate them
rubrics_metrics.description: Give group members explicit roles (e.g., starter/scribe, moderator, reporter, spy, information seeker, critic, scheduler) so everyone has an important way to contribute and productive behaviors are elevated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roles delegate authority to students, promote collaboration, and disrupt classroom hierarchies. Rotate roles every session so all students take on high-status roles (e.g., reporting). Teach students how to fulfill roles and plan time for practice. Examples of roles and responsibilities are provided verbatim in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track and ensure role variety across the semester
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students track their use of different roles and require that all students take each role at least once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice (described via Johanna Rämö's implementation) ensures equity in role experience and status; track role assignments and monitor compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervene when students fall into the same roles
rubrics_metrics.description: If you observe the same students always occupying particular roles (e.g., marker-holder, frequent sharer), explicitly prompt role redistribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit prompts to mix up engagement: e.g., 'Marcus, why don’t you give another student a chance to work on the white board?' or request someone who didn't share last time to report this time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use whole-class discussion intentionally and after student thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Whole-class discussions are ideal for synthesizing mathematical ideas and comparing perspectives, but they tend to be inequitable unless intentionally facilitated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide students time to think (via partner/group work) before whole-class discussion so more students can contribute. Intentionally select and connect student ideas and representations and frame discussions around learning criteria to build evaluative judgement. Avoid beginning new topics with whole-class discussion, which privileges students already familiar with the topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use whole-class discussion to reshape status hierarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat whole-class discussion as a venue for elevating students publicly and challenging existing status orders in the classroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select student ideas purposefully to broaden who is seen as competent; be mindful that public stakes are higher and some students fear humiliation—use facilitation strategies to create safer public participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gallery walk to make student work public and spark movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a gallery of student work (posters, boards) and have students circulate to observe and respond, using guiding questions tailored to the mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicalities: requires wall/room space; typical time 5–15 minutes. Provide guiding prompts (examples: 'What do you notice in how other groups approached the problem?', 'What do you wonder?'). Variation: poster-session format where one member stays at each poster then rotate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Everyone Shares as a low-stakes synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Have every student share a very brief (one-sentence) contribution to ensure universal voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as synthesis after another activity (e.g., gallery walk) and keep contributions concise to maintain pace. Good for test review, reporting struggles, or key takeaways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper Toss to introduce anonymity and randomness
rubrics_metrics.description: Students write a response to a guiding question on a sheet, crumple and toss it; then pick up others’ papers to read or add to anonymously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple toss rounds; options include adding a question or commentary on picked-up paper. Benefits: anonymity reduces fear of failure and lets students report on others' thinking. Can be run in about five minutes and used as an entry to whole-class discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make student work public with whiteboards and low-tech alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use wall whiteboards/blackboards or cheap melamine panels to encourage public writing, collaboration, and sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public artifacts support collaboration, revision, and feedback. Cheap whiteboards can be made from melamine panels cut to size. Use boards for semi-anonymous check-ins (prompts like 'How are you feeling today?', 'What is the big idea?'). Provide markers/chalk and support reluctant writers by handing them a marker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage virtual structures for parallel and anonymous participation
rubrics_metrics.description: In synchronous online settings, use chat and collaborative tools to create parallel conversations and anonymous participation options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage chat responses, then invite specific students to speak to elevate status. Tools: Google Drive/Sheets, Jamboard, Padlet. These allow instructors to monitor many groups at once and let students work with anonymity, often increasing participation compared to verbal contributions alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume some students feel unsafe; co-construct a welcoming space and do not force participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize prior trauma and the disciplinary culture of mathematics that makes some students hesitant; avoid explanations like 'students are shy' that absolve instructors from responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that negative stereotypical behaviors (calling things trivial, fast lecturing, always calling on the first hand) reinforce exclusion. Co-construct community agreements, invite students but do not force participation, and accept that some may choose not to speak while creating safer avenues for contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask questions that elicit thinking and support academically productive talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Use questions to communicate valued mathematical thinking and to facilitate students doing the thinking themselves; prefer academically productive talk over Initiate-Response-Evaluate (IRE) exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of productive prompts: 'How are you thinking about this problem?', 'What are your initial ideas?', 'Where are you getting stuck?', 'Does this look like anything we’ve done before?'. These elicit reasoning without immediate evaluation and help students articulate thinking publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask students to comment on peers' thinking after peer discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: After partner or small-group work, ask students to report on or evaluate peers' ideas as a way to invite participation without sole ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample prompts: 'What was something interesting your peer shared?', 'Did you get any new ideas from your partner?', 'Can someone tell me what your group talked about?', 'Did your group have a consensus, or different ideas?' These are process-oriented and lower-risk for participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice active listening and use nonjudgmental acknowledgements
rubrics_metrics.description: When students share, avoid immediate judgment (falling back into IRE). Use active listening and responses that further conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonjudgmental acknowledgements include nodding, open posture, and phrases like: 'That’s interesting, thanks for sharing.'; 'You mentioned X, and I would love if you could explain more about that.'; 'Could you tell me more about...?' ; 'Does anyone have any questions for our speaker?' These responses focus on extending rather than evaluating student contributions.
